- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.7) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment turns negative (≤0.3) or shows sharp decline, model often overcorrects upward; adjust downward bias, especially after spikes.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to mean-revert; apply downward drag or reduce forecast slope for next 5–7 days.
- When sentiment is neutral or flat (0.0–0.3), model often fails to capture mean reversion; use recent 7-day average as baseline for correction.
- If forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows early divergence (e.g., first 3–5 days), model may be lagging; adjust for early correction if sentiment is weak.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is positive but price has not yet peaked, model may overestimate; apply “sentiment-adjusted decay” to forecast tail.
- If sentiment is negative and price is rising, model often misreads sentiment; reduce forecast by 5–10% if sentiment <0.4 and price > previous peak.
- If forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows volatility, model may be underestimating risk; add 2–3% volatility buffer if sentiment is neutral or negative.
